title: Diana Edulji Calls for Harmanpreet Kaur's Removal as T20I Captain After World Cup Exit
excerpt: Former India captain and ICC Hall of Famer says Harmanpreet has 'stagnated' and demands bold leadership changes after a second consecutive group-stage elimination at the Women's T20 World Cup.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Diana Edulji calls for Harmanpreet Kaur's removal as T20I captain after World Cup exit.
  • India faced consecutive group-stage eliminations at the Women's T20 World Cup 2026.
  • Mithali Raj supports Smriti Mandhana for ODI captaincy and suggests younger candidates for T20I.
  • BCCI retained Harmanpreet as captain for the Asian Games despite criticism.
  • India dropped 11 catches during the tournament, ranking third-worst in the competition.

  • Former India captain Diana Edulji has called for Harmanpreet Kaur to be replaced as T20I captain, saying she has "stagnated" in the role.
  • India suffered a second consecutive group-stage exit at the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 in England, losing to South Africa and Australia.
  • Mithali Raj has backed Smriti Mandhana for the ODI captaincy and suggested Shafali Verma or Jemimah Rodrigues for the T20I role.
  • Despite the criticism, the BCCI's selection committee retained Harmanpreet as captain for the upcoming Asian Games.

Edulji Delivers Blunt Verdict on Harmanpreet's Captaincy

Diana Edulji, one of the most decorated figures in Indian women's cricket, has issued a stinging call for India to move on from Harmanpreet Kaur as T20I captain following the team's elimination from the ICC Women's T20 World Cup 2026 in England.

The former India captain and ICC Hall of Famer, who also served on the BCCI's Committee of Administrators, told Cricbuzz that while Harmanpreet remained her favourite player, the time for change had arrived.

"I think we should look beyond Harman. Though she is my favourite player and I've always supported her, I think we need to move on, at least in the T20Is. Let her continue as a player and think about a new captain."

— Diana Edulji, former India captain

Edulji was particularly pointed in her assessment of Harmanpreet's tactical leadership. "We should have someone with a few better ideas, especially in terms of strategy. Also, bowling changes — there's a lot more that goes into the captaincy. I think she's stagnated now," she said.

A Pattern of ICC Disappointment

India's exit in England marks a second successive group-stage elimination at a T20 World Cup under Harmanpreet's leadership, following the 2024 debacle. Despite possessing one of the strongest talent pools in women's cricket, the team has repeatedly failed to convert potential into results on the biggest stage.

"Her format is T20Is."</p><cite>— Mithali Raj, former India captain</cite></blockquote> <p>Vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has also signalled her readiness."

An earlier loss to South Africa hurt India's campaign, but it was the defeat to Australia in their final group match — when a win would have taken them through to the semifinals — that sealed their fate. India's fielding was particularly dire: the team dropped 11 catches across the tournament, the third-worst record in the competition, with seven players responsible.

Edulji also questioned specific selection decisions during the tournament, including the use of Yastika Bhatia as a non-bowling, non-batting second wicketkeeper. "She couldn't come out to bat. She's not a bowler. So, it was a wasted position," Edulji said.

Growing Chorus for Leadership Change

Edulji is not alone in calling for a captaincy shake-up. Mithali Raj, India's all-time leading run-scorer in women's cricket, told PTI that the captaincy should be split across formats.

"With the vast experience that she (Smriti) has, at least the one-day and Test format should be given to her and perhaps the T20 to someone younger. I think Shafali Verma. Her format is T20Is."

— Mithali Raj, former India captain

Vice-captain Smriti Mandhana has also signalled her readiness. In a recent interview with The Times of India, Mandhana — who has served as Harmanpreet's deputy since 2016 — was asked if she was ready to lead. Her answer was unequivocal: "I am ready."

Mithali added a crucial caveat, regardless of who is appointed: "Whoever they pick, they need to give them some time to settle." That emphasis on continuity stands in contrast to what both she and Mandhana have described as a reactive approach, with Mithali bluntly saying, "We don't have a roadmap. We are only thinking series to series."

Selectors Stand Firm — For Now

Edulji's criticism carried extra sting because of its timing. Her comments came on the same day the Amita Sharma-headed selection committee retained Harmanpreet as captain for the upcoming Asian Games. Asked whether she was comfortable with that decision, Edulji was categorical: "No, I'm not."

She also drew a sharp parallel with the men's setup, where the BCCI recently replaced Suryakumar Yadav as T20I captain with Shreyas Iyer despite Suryakumar having led the side to a World Cup title. "If we can take bold decisions in men's cricket, I think we should take bold decisions in women's cricket as well," Edulji said.

The former captain did not limit her critique to Harmanpreet. She called for head coach Amol Muzumdar to be replaced, saying, "I don't see him being able to produce anything more now than what he has already done." She also questioned fielding coach Munish Bali's impact and urged the BCCI to build separate squads, coaching setups, and captains for the T20I and ODI formats.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, many of whom watched the World Cup matches live in England, the debate over Harmanpreet's captaincy resonates beyond cricket. The Indian women's team's growing profile — amplified by the Women's Premier League and the team's 2025 ODI World Cup triumph — has built a passionate global fan base that expects results to match investment. The team's Olympic qualification offers a silver lining, but the captaincy question will dominate the conversation in the months ahead.

What Comes Next

With the Asian Games on the horizon and the Olympics now confirmed, the BCCI faces a decision that will define the next cycle of Indian women's cricket. Edulji, for one, is worried that inaction will perpetuate the problem. "If we win the Asian Games and come back with another medal, the same story will continue — that this group carries on for another series. And it will never end," she warned.

Whether the selectors act on the mounting pressure from legends of the game or back Harmanpreet through the Asian Games and into the Olympic cycle, the status quo has been unmistakably challenged. Two group-stage exits, 11 dropped catches, and a growing queue of credible successors have made this the loudest the captaincy debate has ever been in Indian women's cricket.
